name: Obadiah
sourceNote: Translated from the Hebrew Masoretic Text as given in the Westminster Leningrad Codex (Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible edition), with the Septuagint (Old Greek) consulted. Obadiah, the shortest book of the Old Testament, is a single chapter of twenty-one verses directed against Edom; it most likely reflects Edom’s conduct when Babylon destroyed Jerusalem in 587/586 BC (compare Psalm 137:7). Verses 1–9 closely parallel Jeremiah 49:7–22. Among the ancient manuscripts, as reported in the published editions, parts of Obadiah survive in the Wadi Murabbaʿat scroll of the Twelve (Mur 88) and in the Greek Minor Prophets Scroll from Nahal Hever (8HevXIIgr); these generally support the Masoretic Text. Verse numbers are the same in English and Hebrew.

verses.text:
The vision of Obadiah.{a}
This is what the Lord Yahweh says about Edom—
a report we have heard from Yahweh,
and a messenger is sent out among the nations:
“Up! Let us go to war against her!”—

“Look, I am making you small among the nations;
you will be utterly despised.

The arrogance of your heart has deceived you,
you who dwell in the clefts of the rock,{b}
whose dwelling is on the heights,
who say in your heart,
‘Who can bring me down to the ground?’

Though you fly high as the eagle,
though you place your nest among the stars,
even from there I will pull you down,”
declares Yahweh.

“Had thieves come to you,
or robbers in the night—
how you are ruined!—
would they not have stolen just enough for themselves?
Had grape pickers come to you,
would they not have left some gleanings?

How Esau has been ransacked,
his hidden treasures sought out!

“Because of the violence done to your brother Jacob,
shame will cover you,
and you will be cut off forever.

In the day you stood by, at a distance,
in the day aliens took away his riches,
when foreigners passed through his gates
and threw lots over Jerusalem,
you as well were one of them.

But you should not have stared in glee{f} on your brother’s day,
on the day of his disaster;
you should not have exulted over Judah’s people
in the day of their destruction,
nor opened wide your mouth
in the day of trouble.

You should never have waited at the fork in the road{h}
to kill his escaping refugees,
or surrendered his survivors
on the day of disaster.

“For the day of Yahweh is near
upon all the nations.
As you have done, it will be done to you;
your deeds will return on your own head.

Jacob’s family will become a blaze,
Joseph’s family a flame,
and Esau’s family dry straw;
they will ignite it and burn it up,
and no one in Esau’s family will survive.
Yahweh has said so.

“The people of the Negev{k} shall take the mount of Esau as their own,
and those of the Shephelah{l} the Philistines’ land;
Ephraim’s fields and Samaria’s fields they shall possess,
and Benjamin shall have Gilead.

Deliverers{o} will go up on Mount Zion
to rule the mount of Esau,
and the kingdom will be Yahweh’s.

notes.text: The name means “servant of Yahweh.” Nothing else is known of the prophet; he is not to be identified with the Obadiah of 1 Kings 18.
Hebrew selaʿ, “rock,” perhaps also alluding to Sela, an Edomite stronghold (2 Kings 14:7). Edom’s mountain strongholds, south and east of the Dead Sea, were hard to reach.
The meaning of the Hebrew mazor is uncertain; perhaps “a net” or “a wound.” The Hebrew text reads “your bread”; some, with a small addition, read “those who eat your bread.”
Edom was proverbial for its wisdom (Jeremiah 49:7; compare Job 2:11, where Eliphaz is from Teman).
A region or chief city of Edom.
Hebrew “do not gloat.” The eight prohibitions in verses 12–14 have the force of a reproach for what Edom has already done.
Hebrew ʾed, “calamity,” here three times, sounds like the name Edom.
The meaning of the Hebrew pereq is uncertain; perhaps “the breach” or “the mountain pass.”
“You” is plural here, perhaps addressing Judah, which drank the cup of God’s wrath (compare Jeremiah 25:15–29), or Edom, which caroused on Mount Zion after its fall.
So the Hebrew; the Septuagint and Vulgate, with different vowels, read “will dispossess those who dispossessed them.”
The dry southern region of Judah.
The low hills between the Judean highlands and the coastal plain.
A Phoenician town between Tyre and Sidon (1 Kings 17:9). The Hebrew of the first two lines is difficult.
Probably Sardis in Asia Minor. In later Jewish usage the name was applied to Spain, hence “Sephardic” Jews.
Or “Those who have been delivered,” following the Septuagint and Syriac.
